title: quake
text: Quake is a FPS game made by id software and released in 1996. it stood put among the FPS or "Doom Clones" at the time for a few notable reasons. It was fully 3D, had smooth animations and complex (for its time) level design. But how does it hold up? How does it play for a first time player? The awnser to both is amazingly well. Game: The game is set across 4 different dimensions. This causes each of the four episodes to have its own unique location. The weapons are plentifull and fun to use. The line-up includes grenade launchers, nail guns and a lightning gun. The only problem I had with the game was the two bossfights. They didn't require shooting, but pressing buttons. You may have to shoot you way to the buttons, but the bosses themselves doesn't require one bullet to kill, which really sucks. The games difficulty is on the heavy side. I played on normal and found the difficulty what I would expect on hard with other games. Respect to the people finding nightmare enjoyable and finishable.. Technical: The game works out of the box with the steam version, but there are a few issues. The controls are not as smooth as modern FPS games. The soundtrack ran off a cd, that means no soundtrack for the steam version. the resolution is really low (Doesn't bother me but can bother you). To fix all three issues mentiones above (The only technical complaints I had) I used the Ultimate quake patch. It uses the DarkPlaces engine developed by LordHavoc, the plasmagun fix by OoPpEe, the music patch originally hosted on and the NSIS install system by Nullsoft. The Ultimate Quake Patch was compiled by (as I understand it) MenaceInc. I would highly recommend this game to ANYONE!! P.S. Don't forget to download episode 5. Its calles DOPA and was developed by Machine Games (Who did a amazing job with Wolfenstein the New Order and Wolfenstein the Old Blood) for quakes 20th birthday. It has te same old school design and if it was included with the original game, I wouldnt have know that it wasn't id that made this episode.I can't think of higher praise for DOPA. Get it if you get Quake. It was released for free. To install it you just have to create a dopa folder where quake is instelled, extract the zipfile in the folder and double click the batch file.

text: I loved this game when I first played it long ago, and I love it still. The story, while ground breaking at the time, is non-existant by today's standards. That's a good thing. An FPS should be about barreling down a hallway, screaming obscenities and hurling death-vortexes at your foes, not searching for a better script and having romantic conversations with your hand. Lookin' at you, Bionic Commando. The game is simple, and that's all an FPS really needs. None of this pretentious carp about how the outcome of WWII depends of a single soldier who seems to miraculously heal by crouching behind walls. In Q2, you're a sometimes too-fragile sack of meat, guns, and testosterone-plated armor. You get riddled with bullets, blast your way through an entire alien army, and then escape in style. Does a game need more?

text: Quake III Arena is one hell of a game. I grew up on the Unreal side and so I'm a little biased towards that series, but I still love the Quake series and this game is still amazing in comparison to UT99 and all on its own. A crowning achievement for arena FPS, multiplayer FPS and for iD. ++Totally skill-based deathmatch galore. Git gud, or git rekt. Balanced, competitive gameplay but easily accessible to casuals. ++Weapons deliver power and will destroy opponents when used right. Great arsenal and impactful feel. +Movement is a joy and is key to success +Gore is great +The amount of characters from iD games over the years is awesome +Sound design is decent +Brilliant graphics with impressive texture work and animations +Runs very well on modern systems without any tweaking necessary (unless you want HD resolutions and higher FOV, of course) +Awesome music +-N/A -The AI is just aim-botty on the hardest difficulty -Maps aren't too visually diverse, even if the artstyle is good -Too light on gameplay customisation -Short campaign --An expensive add-on (Quake III: Team Arena) was released to add maps and game modes that absolutely should have been there from the beginning Sound: 8/10 Graphics: 9/10 Gameplay: 9/10 Content/Replayability: 5/10 (without a community) Overall: 8/10 There's no reason to compare UT99 against this. Both are fantastic in similar ways and for different reasons. It's not anywhere near as much of a must-buy as it most certainly was when it had a community, but even against bots it's still a lot of fun.

text: Not nearly as enjoyable as the first Quake xpac. Don't get me wrong; this is still playable, but the level design suffers here. The original game (and the first xpac) did an excellent job with the layouts of the stages; they would show you a Silver Key Door that you couldn't unlock yet, but then they'd present you with an alternate path that would eventually lead to the Silver Key (so you always had a sense of progression / where to go next). In this xpac, I found the levels to be labyrinthine and frustrating, especially some of the elevator puzzles. The levels are also unfortunately littered with ammo, (uber-)guns, and powerups. It's too much; the encounters start to lose their variety when you're always loaded with infinite ammo for the most overpowered guns. After the 100th time of rounding a corner and blasting a fiend/death knight in the face with a rocket/plasma, the exhilaration wanes. Recommended only for the completionist.

title: quantum conundrum
text: A Spiritual successor to the Portal series, Quantum Conundrum retains the core theme of puzzle solving based around a central mechanic. In Portal, this was the use of the portal gun. In Quantum Conundrum, you get access to a dimensional altering glove that allows you to jump between 4, technically 5 if you count normal, alternate dimensions. Each dimension alters the world around you and it is up to you to figure out how to use each dimensional change to solve puzzles and move throughout the manor. Fluffy dimension changes everything to be made out of pillows, heavy changes everything into solid metal. Slow motion and anti gravity are self explanatory. Each one allows you to interact with it differently, such as in fluffy, you can pick up just about any object, allowing you to move normally massive objects in order to activate switches or build staircases. The wiiting and voice acting are solid, if unspectacular. The primary voice actor is John de Lancie, best known for his roles on Star Trek as Q, and more recently as Discord in My Little Pony, and Alarak in StarCraft II. He portrays a crack inventor who created the dimensional device and will guide you through the manor with helpful tips or observations. While not his best work, de Lancie does an admirable job, and it certainly lends the game some needed personality. Overall, Quantum Conundrum is a decent job of trying to carry on the Portal legacy. The characters aren't as standout as GlaDOS or Cave, but it does well. Sadly the studio is now defunct, so we likely won't ever get a sequel Recommended for those who enjoyed Portal and are looking for something in a similar vein.
